issues.legal_issue: Continuous, intentional harassment that humiliates a person and is closely followed by that person’s suicide can amount to abetment of suicide rather than merely insult or intimidation.
material_facts: The victim was repeatedly taunted and humiliated by the accused, including through remarks that mocked her broken engagement and addressed her as a relative’s wife.
The harassment was not a solitary incident; the victim’s family described it as recurrent, and the victim had expressed that she could no longer tolerate it and might end her life.
The victim was visibly distressed after the final episode of taunting, wept through the night, and died by suicide the following morning.
Witness testimony supported the allegations of repeated conduct and the final encounter; the Court found the conduct intentional and directed at humiliating the victim.
issues.conclusion: The repeated, intentional humiliation and taunting amounted to instigation and abetment of suicide under Section 306 IPC, not merely insult or intimidation; the conviction of the appellants other than the juvenile appellant was upheld.
issues.legal_principle: Sections 306 and 107 IPC govern abetment of suicide and abetment generally. Abetment requires instigation, conspiracy accompanied by an act or illegal omission, or intentional aid. Instigation may be express or implied and may be inferred from a continuing course of conduct; in a suicide case, the evidence must establish direct or indirect incitement, a positive act sufficiently proximate to the suicide, and the accused’s requisite mental element. Mere harassment, an isolated casual remark, or words spoken in anger do not alone suffice. The court assesses the whole context, including the conduct’s effect on the victim and whether it created a situation in which the victim perceived no other option. The Court relied on Ramesh Kumar v. State of Chhattisgarh, State of W.B. v. Orilal Jaiswal, Pawan Kumar v. State of Himachal Pradesh, Madan Mohan Singh v. State of Gujarat, S.S. Chheena v. Vijay Kumar Mahajan, Chitresh Kumar Chopra v. State (Govt. of NCT of Delhi), and Amalendu Pal v. State of W.B.; it also referred to the constitutional dignity and equality principles discussed in Pawan Kumar.

rule.if: criminal_appeal_from_conviction and suicide_occurred and repeated_humiliating_conduct and victim_expressed_intolerable_distress and final_conduct_proximate_to_suicide and evidence_supports_intentional_instigation

predicates.criminal_appeal_from_conviction: The accused appealed a criminal conviction for conduct alleged to have abetted a person’s suicide.
predicates.suicide_occurred: The person subjected to the alleged conduct died by suicide.
predicates.repeated_humiliating_conduct: The accused repeatedly directed taunts or other humiliating conduct at the person, rather than engaging in only a solitary or casual exchange.
predicates.victim_expressed_intolerable_distress: The person expressed that the repeated conduct was unbearable or indicated an intention to die.
predicates.final_conduct_proximate_to_suicide: A final episode of the conduct occurred shortly before the person died by suicide.
predicates.evidence_supports_intentional_instigatio: Evidence supported that the accused intentionally engaged in conduct calculated to provoke, pressure, or drive the person toward suicide.

issues.definition: When a criminal appeal concerns a suicide and the stated facts establish repeated intentional humiliation, expressed distress, and a closely proximate final episode, the rule upholds a conviction for abetment of suicide.

issues.legal_issue: A person who was under eighteen when the offence was committed may claim the benefit of juvenile justice law at the appellate stage, and an established claim entitles that person to the benefit of that law.
material_facts: A certificate recording the appellant’s date of birth showed that he was under eighteen on the dates of the alleged conduct.
The certificate was not disputed, and the Court found no reason to doubt it or require a further inquiry.
The appellant raised the claim of juvenility before the Supreme Court, although it had not been raised before the trial court or the High Court.
issues.conclusion: The appellant was entitled to the benefit of the Juvenile Justice (Care and Protection of Children) Act, 2000; the conviction and High Court order concerning him were set aside and the proceedings against him were terminated.
issues.legal_principle: Sections 2(k), 2(l), 7A and 20 of the Juvenile Justice (Care and Protection of Children) Act, 2000, as amended, entitle a person who had not completed eighteen years on the date of the offence to the benefit of the Act. Under Section 7A, a claim of juvenility may be raised at any stage, including before the Supreme Court. The Court relied on Raju v. State of Haryana and the authorities discussed there, including Hari Ram v. State of Rajasthan, Mohan Mali v. State of Madhya Pradesh, Daya Nand v. State of Haryana, Dharambir v. State (NCT of Delhi), Jitendra Singh @ Babboo Singh v. State of Uttar Pradesh, Abuzar Hossain v. State of West Bengal, and Abdul Razzaq v. State of Uttar Pradesh.

rule.if: criminal_appeal_from_conviction and age_under_eighteen_at_offence and reliable_age_evidence and juvenility_claim_raised_on_appeal

predicates.criminal_appeal_from_conviction: The person appealed a criminal conviction in proceedings concerning an alleged offence.
predicates.age_under_eighteen_at_offence: The person had not completed eighteen years of age when the alleged offence was committed.
predicates.reliable_age_evidence: Documentary or inquiry evidence reliably established the person’s age at the relevant time.
predicates.juvenility_claim_raised_on_appeal: The person raised the claim of being underage before an appellate court, although it had not been raised earlier.

issues.definition: When an appellant in a criminal conviction proceeding reliably establishes that they were under eighteen at the time of the offence and raises juvenility on appeal, the rule grants juvenile-law benefit and terminates the proceedings as stated.
